key_terms.meaning: μ_i = (∂G/∂n_i) at fixed T, P and other moles; it is the partial molar Gibbs energy.
For each species i, μ_i in every phase must be equal at fixed T and P.
M̄_i = (∂(nM)/∂n_i) at fixed T, P and other moles; the change in total property when one mole of i is added.
V̄_i = (∂V/∂n_i) at fixed T, P and other moles; the volume contribution per mole of i in the mixture.
Σ n_i dM̄_i = 0 at fixed T and P, or Σ x_i dM̄_i = 0; partial molar properties are not independent.
The corrected pressure that keeps μ_i = μ_i⁰ + RT ln(f_i/f_i⁰) valid for real fluids.
φ_i = f_i/(x_iP) for a mixture; φ_i → 1 as P → 0.
A solution that follows f_i = x_i f_i^pure at all T, P and composition, with zero excess volume and zero heat of mixing.
f_i = x_i f_i^pure; the fugacity of a component in an ideal solution is its mole fraction times its pure fugacity.
M^E = M − M^ideal at the same T, P and composition; it measures departure from ideal-solution behavior.
ΔM_mix = M(solution) − Σ x_i M_i^pure; for an ideal solution ΔV_mix = 0 and ΔH_mix = 0.
a_i = f_i/f_i⁰; it replaces mole fraction in μ_i = μ_i⁰ + RT ln a_i.
γ_i = a_i/x_i; it measures liquid-phase nonideality and tends to 1 in the Lewis-Randall standard state.
An excess Gibbs energy model, for example G^E/RT = x1x2(A21x1 + A12x2), used to obtain activity coefficients.
A two-parameter excess Gibbs model G^E/RT = A12A21x1x2/(A12x1 + A21x2) for binary activity coefficients.
A local-composition model G^E/RT = −Σ x_i ln(Σ x_j Λ_ij) used for activity coefficients of miscible mixtures.
For vapor-liquid equilibrium, μ_i^V = μ_i^L, equivalently f_i^V = f_i^L for each component.
y_iP = γ_i x_i P_i^sat for low-pressure VLE with ideal vapor and nonideal liquid.
For a closed system of fixed initial composition, specifying two independent intensive variables fixes the equilibrium state.
The limit of γ_i as x_i → 0; it characterizes dilute-component nonideality and helps fit models.

takeaways: Chemical potential is the partial molar Gibbs energy, and equality of μ_i across phases is the equilibrium condition.
Partial molar properties describe how a mixture property changes when one component is added at fixed T, P and other amounts.
The Gibbs-Duhem equation ties partial molar properties together, so they cannot all be varied independently.
Fugacity preserves the simple chemical-potential formula for real gases, and φ_i measures gas nonideality.
An ideal solution follows the Lewis-Randall rule, while real solutions deviate and need activity coefficients.
Excess properties and property changes of mixing show how far a real mixture is from ideal-solution behavior.
Activity replaces mole fraction in the chemical potential, and γ_i = a_i/x_i is the practical measure of liquid nonideality.
Margules, van Laar and Wilson models convert excess Gibbs energy information into activity coefficients for VLE calculations.
bank_note: The syllabi stress derivations and numerical use of chemical potential, fugacity and activity, Gibbs-Duhem consistency, excess properties, activity coefficient models and VLE calculations.

bank.q: Define chemical potential and state the phase-equilibrium criterion for a species present in two phases. Explain why the criterion uses μ rather than concentration.
outline: Definition of μ as partial molar Gibbs energy
Equality of μ_i in all phases at equilibrium
Derivation from dG at fixed T and P
Concentration alone is insufficient because μ includes standard state and nonideality

bank.q: Explain partial molar property M̄_i. Give the relation between total mixture property M and partial molar properties, and describe one way to measure partial molar volume.
outline: Definition as derivative at fixed T, P and other moles
Relation M = Σ x_i M̄_i
Physical meaning of adding one mole of component i
Intercept method on a V versus mole-fraction plot

bank.q: Write the Gibbs-Duhem equation for a mixture at fixed T and P. State what it says about partial molar properties and give one consequence for activity coefficients.
outline: Equation Σ x_i dM̄_i = 0 or Σ n_i dM̄_i = 0
Partial molar properties are not independent
For activity coefficients Σ x_i d ln γ_i = 0 at fixed T and P
Use in consistency testing

bank.q: Define fugacity and fugacity coefficient for a pure gas and for a component in a gas mixture. State the limiting values as P → 0.
outline: Fugacity replaces pressure in the chemical-potential formula
Pure gas φ = f/P
Mixture φ_i = f_i/(x_iP)
φ → 1 and φ_i → 1 as P → 0
Fugacity has pressure units

bank.q: Starting from μ_i = μ_i⁰ + RT ln(f_i/f_i⁰), derive ln φ_i = (μ_i − μ_i^ideal-gas)/RT for a component in a mixture. State each term.
outline: Ideal-gas chemical potential μ_i^ig = μ_i⁰ + RT ln(x_iP/P⁰)
Subtract ideal-gas expression from real expression
φ_i = f_i/(x_iP)
Residual chemical potential relation
Use of an equation of state to compute φ_i

bank.q: For low-pressure vapor-liquid equilibrium, derive the modified Raoult's law y_iP = γ_i x_i P_i^sat and list the assumptions.
outline: Equate fugacities in vapor and liquid
Ideal vapor: φ_i^V = 1
Liquid fugacity written with activity coefficient
Approximate pure-liquid fugacity by P_i^sat
Assumptions: low pressure, ideal vapor, negligible Poynting correction

bank.q: For a binary two-suffix Margules model G^E/RT = A x1x2, derive ln γ1 and ln γ2 and show that they satisfy Gibbs-Duhem.
outline: Use ln γ_i = ∂(nG^E/RT)/∂n_i
Obtain ln γ1 = A x2² and ln γ2 = A x1²
Check Σ x_i d ln γ_i = 0
Interpret sign of A as positive or negative deviation

bank.q: Calculate ΔG_mix, ΔS_mix and ΔH_mix for an ideal solution from x1, x2 and T. Explain why ΔV_mix and ΔH_mix are zero.
outline: ΔG_mix = RT Σ x_i ln x_i
ΔS_mix = −R Σ x_i ln x_i
ΔH_mix = 0 for ideal solution
ΔV_mix = 0 for ideal solution
Link to zero excess enthalpy and zero excess volume

bank.q: Use experimental VLE data at low pressure to calculate activity coefficients, then test them with the Gibbs-Duhem consistency relation for a binary system.
outline: Calculate γ_i = y_iP/(x_iP_i^sat)
Calculate both components from data
Apply Gibbs-Duhem point or integral test
Plot or compare ln γ1 and ln γ2
State likely sources of inconsistency

bank.q: Compare ideal solution, Lewis-Randall rule and real solution behavior. Explain positive and negative deviations from Raoult's law with molecular reasons.
outline: Ideal solution follows Lewis-Randall rule
Real solutions have γ_i not equal to 1
Positive deviation: γ > 1, weaker unlike interactions
Negative deviation: γ < 1, stronger unlike interactions
Azeotropes may appear

bank.q: Derive the Gibbs-Duhem equation from the definition of partial molar properties. Use it to show that activity coefficients in a binary mixture are not independent.
outline: Euler relation M = Σ n_iM̄_i
Differentiate and compare with dM expression
Obtain Σ n_i dM̄_i = 0 at fixed T and P
Apply to M̄_i = μ_i or ln γ_i
Binary relation x1 d ln γ1 + x2 d ln γ2 = 0

bank.q: Discuss fugacity, activity and the VLE criterion. Derive the general isofugacity condition and reduce it to modified Raoult's law for low pressure.
outline: Equilibrium requires equal chemical potential
Equal fugacity for each component
General relation φ_i^V y_iP = γ_i x_i f_i^pure
Low-pressure approximations
Final modified Raoult's law

bank.q: Compare Margules, van Laar and Wilson activity coefficient models. State their assumptions, parameters, strengths and limitations for VLE calculations.
outline: Excess Gibbs energy forms for each model
Number of parameters for a binary system
Wilson uses local composition
Margules and van Laar are empirical
Limitations for liquid-liquid equilibrium and multicomponent use

bank.q: Explain excess properties and property changes of mixing. How do the signs of H^E and V^E indicate nonideality and heat effects?
outline: Definition M^E = M − M^ideal
Definition ΔM_mix = M − Σ x_i M_i^pure
H^E positive means endothermic mixing
H^E negative means exothermic mixing
V^E positive means expansion, negative means contraction

glossary.def: The partial molar Gibbs energy of a species, written μ_i, which determines its equilibrium behavior.
The contribution of one mole of a component to a mixture property at fixed T, P and other amounts.
A relation showing that changes in partial molar properties in a mixture at fixed T and P are not independent.
A corrected pressure that makes the chemical-potential formula valid for real gases and liquids.
The ratio of fugacity to pressure, or to x_iP in a mixture, and it tends to 1 at low pressure.
A solution that obeys the Lewis-Randall rule and has zero excess volume and zero heat of mixing.
The statement f_i = x_i f_i^pure for an ideal solution.
The difference between a real mixture property and its ideal-solution value at the same T, P and composition.
The difference between a solution property and the sum of pure-component properties in the same proportions.
A dimensionless effective fugacity, a_i = f_i/f_i⁰, used in the chemical-potential expression.
The ratio γ_i = a_i/x_i that measures departure from ideal-solution behavior.
For an ideal liquid mixture, p_i = x_i p_i^sat.
For a dilute solute, p_i = x_i k_H, where k_H is the Henry constant.
The low-pressure VLE relation y_iP = γ_i x_i P_i^sat for nonideal liquids.
An excess Gibbs energy model that expresses activity coefficients as a polynomial in mole fractions.
A two-parameter excess Gibbs energy model for binary activity coefficients.
A local-composition activity coefficient model with binary parameters Λ_ij.
The condition in which vapor and liquid phases have equal chemical potential for every component.
A mixture composition at which vapor and liquid have the same composition and cannot be separated by simple distillation.
A check that experimental activity coefficients obey the Gibbs-Duhem relation.
The reference state chosen for chemical potential and activity at a given T and P.
The limiting activity coefficient of a component as its mole fraction goes to zero.
The difference between a real-fluid property and its ideal-gas value at the same T and P.
For a closed system of fixed initial composition, two independent intensive variables determine the equilibrium state.
